text_a: The restated available() rationale states the JDK 26/27 read-ahead gate as "the inflater holds leftover input" when the actual gate is more than 26 bytes of leftover input.
scenario_a: Exactly the body the patch's own new test builds is a counterexample: member + 10-byte bad-magic tail read through a 4096-byte buffer leaves `available() == 0` and `inf.getRemaining() == 18`, and JDK 26/27 do **not** read ahead, contradicting "or the inflater holds leftover input". Anyone reasoning from this sentence about why the concatenated-member mode is JDK-stable will conclude read-ahead happens whenever any bytes are buffered, which is false below 27 leftover bytes.
text_b: The F06 rationale states the JDK 26/27 read-ahead gate as "the source reports more bytes or the inflater holds leftover input", but the real gate is `this.in.available() > 0 || n > 26`; leftover input alone is not enough, and the 26-byte threshold is what actually forces the harness's available() to be honest.
scenario_b: A maintainer reads this javadoc and concludes that FragmentedInputStream.available() only has to be non-zero-ish, or that a pessimistic available() is safe whenever the inflater still holds bytes. They replace the honest delegate with a conservative `return 0;` (a realistic "model a network stream" change) and the concatenated-member mode (mode 2) silently stops round-tripping on JDK 26/27 for every input whose inflater leftover lands at 26 bytes or fewer -- readBody returns only the first member and `check` fails with "returned the wrong body in mode 2", or, worse in a differential sense, the harness quietly stops covering the second member. The sentence as written gives no way to predict the buf=30 case above.

text_a: The C01 fix also changes classification for lists where gzip is not the outermost coding, turning a previously pass-through body into an UncheckedIOException, and nothing pins that half.
scenario_a: A buffering CDN that re-encodes and sends `Content-Encoding: gzip, br` over a gzip-then-brotli body used to surface as a JSON parse error on the raw bytes; it now surfaces as `UncheckedIOException: ZipException: Not in GZIP format` from `readBody`. The change of failure mode is unpinned, so a later reviewer simplifying the loop back to "last coding wins" would break nothing in the suite.
text_b: `header.split(",")` turns an untrusted, provider-sized Content-Encoding value into O(n) String allocations, in the one class that otherwise clamps every untrusted header before letting it size an allocation.
scenario_b: A compromised or buggy provider answers every RPC call with `Content-Encoding: ` followed by ~380 KB of `a,` pairs and a normal small body. Each readBody call now burns ~11 ms of CPU and churns ~13 MB of short-lived objects before deciding the body is not gzip; pre-patch the same header cost a length comparison. At even modest request concurrency that is a self-inflicted allocation storm from a header the client never had to parse token-by-token.

text_a: Removing the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` will not break callers — it will silently rebind `tx.sign(list)` to the by-key `sign(Collection<Signer>)`, flipping positional signing to key-matched signing with no compile error.
scenario_a: Consumer code today: `List<Signer> signers = List.of(feePayer, authority); tx.sign(signers);` binds to `sign(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:784) and signs positionally. That method is now `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)`. When it is removed, `sign(Collection<Signer>)` (Transaction.java:773) is still applicable to a `List`, so the exact same source keeps compiling and now validates and signs by public key. A caller who deliberately relied on positional order — for example signing a message whose slot 0 signer is not the first element, which the deprecated overload permitted — either gets signatures in different slots or a new `IllegalArgumentException` at runtime for an assignment that used to succeed. This is the single most-used signing entry point, and it is the only one of the nine deprecated members with a silently-absorbing sibling: `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)`, `sign(String, SequencedCollection)`, all three `signAndBase64Encode(*, SequencedCollection)` forms and the three deprecated statics have no `Collection` counterpart, so those call sites would fail to compile at removal, which is the behaviour `forRemoval` normally advertises.
text_b: `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` on an ABSTRACT interface method forces a compiler warning on every implementor that they cannot avoid, and the method cannot actually be removed without a second source-incompatible break of `Transaction`.
scenario_b: (a) Warning every implementor must eat. `void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` is abstract, so a third-party `Transaction` MUST declare it. javac enables `[removal]` by default (unlike `deprecation`) and fires it on an override, not just a call. I confirmed this with javac 25.0.2 on a minimal repro and on this repo: compiling sava-core's main source set at 1dded1d^ gives 0 warnings; at 1dded1d it gives   BaseTransaction.java:183: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal   BaseTransaction.java:189: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>,byte[],int,int,int) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal A consumer whose build uses `-Werror` (or Gradle `options.compilerArgs.add("-Werror")`, common in library projects) stops compiling on upgrade at their own `@Override public void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`. Their only escapes are annotating their override `@Deprecated` — which propagates the warning to all of their callers — or `@SuppressWarnings("removal")`. This commit added neither annotation anywhere: not on BaseTransaction.java:183, not on PreV1InterfaceShapeTests.java:70, not on SigningCountTests.java:540. (b) The removal is not reachable additively. `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` at :845 holds no implementation — the implementation lives in each implementor's override of the method being removed. Delete :784 and :845's body has nothing to call, so `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` must become abstract. Adding an abstract method to `Transaction` is precisely the break `PreV1InterfaceShapeTests` exists to prevent (its class javadoc: "Everything v1 added to those interfaces must therefore arrive as a `default`... adding an abstract method without one stops this file compiling, which is the published-library rule enforced by the compiler"). So the `forRemoval = true` at :784 schedules a break the repo's own compatibility pin forbids.

text_a: Five of the six new `signInOrder` instance methods bypass `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` and delegate straight to the deprecated members, so overriding the surviving name yields an internally inconsistent object today and a silent behaviour flip when the deprecated names are removed.
scenario_a: A consumer follows MIGRATION.md and migrates their `Transaction` implementation to the surviving name:      @Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> s) { auditLog(s); Transaction.super.signInOrder(s); }  `myTx.signInOrder(signers)` runs the override (:845 -> :846 -> abstract `sign(SequencedCollection)`). `myTx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does NOT: :855 -> :856 calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` at :801, whose body is `setRecentBlockHash(...); sign(signers);` -> the abstract seam. The override never runs and the transaction is signed with no audit record. Same for `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(signers)` (:850 -> :851 -> `signAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` at :791 -> `sign(signers)`), `signInOrder(String, ...)` (:860), and both blockhash Base64 variants (:865, :870). Only 1 of 6 entry points sees the override. The identical move on the by-key side works: overriding `signByKey(Collection)` at :883 IS honoured by :888, :894, :900, :906 and :912, because those funnel through it. Nothing at the declarations says the two families differ, and the one-line javadocs at :854/:859/:864/:869 never name the method they delegate to. Then, when the deprecated members at :791/:801/:811/:822/:833 are removed, those five bodies must be re-pointed at `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` — at which point the consumer's override starts running on all six paths. That is a behaviour change delivered BY the removal, which is exactly what a deprecation cycle exists to avoid.
text_b: Five of the six new `signInOrder*` instance defaults route through the deprecated `sign*` chain instead of through `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`, so an override of the new positional name is honoured by only one of its six entry points — the opposite of the `signByKey` family, where all six funnel through `signByKey(Collection)`.
scenario_b: A consumer implementing `Transaction` migrates off the `forRemoval` name by overriding the new one: `@Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers) { audit(signers); super.signInOrder(signers); }`. `tx.signInOrder(signers)` runs the audit. `tx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does not — it calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` (Transaction.java:856), which calls `setRecentBlockHash` then the abstract `sign(signers)`, never touching the override. A second consequence: because every `signInOrder*` default body is written purely in terms of members marked `forRemoval`, none of them has a body that survives removal, so MIGRATION.md:106-107's "New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides" stops being true the moment the deprecated members go.

text_a: The new migration section invites consumers to use instructions as HashMap/HashSet keys without saying that `equals` throws for the same unvalidated spans the new `hashCode` was deliberately made total for, and nothing pins that throw.
scenario_a: `byte[] data = {1, 2}; var a = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACC), data, 0, 4); var b = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACC), data, 0, 4);` — both permitted, since `createInstruction` is documented as retaining "the supplied array and span without validation". Both take the fallback branch, which is fully deterministic in programId, accounts, array identity, offset and len, so `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` exactly. `new HashSet<Instruction>()` then `add(a); add(b);` reaches `HashMap.putVal`, whose bucket probe calls `b.equals(a)` on the exact hash match, which calls `Arrays.equals(data, 0, 4, data, 0, 4)` and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Array index out of range: 4`. Same for `map.get(b)` after `map.put(a, v)`, and for `offset = -1` (`Array index out of range: -1`). A consumer following this section's advice therefore gets an unchecked exception out of `HashSet.add`.
text_b: The new migration section and interface doc direct consumers to use instructions as HashMap/HashSet keys without saying that equals throws for the unvalidated spans whose hash this commit deliberately preserved, so a lookup can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from inside the collection.
scenario_b: byte[] arr = {1}; var a = Instruction.createInstruction(program, List.of(), arr, 0, 2); var b = Instruction.createInstruction(program, List.of(), arr, 0, 2); var set = new HashSet<Instruction>(); set.add(a); set.contains(b); — a and b take the fallback hash branch and hash identically (same array identity, same offset/len, value-based AccountMeta hash), so the bucket hit calls b.equals(a), which reaches Arrays.equals(arr, 0, 2, arr, 0, 2) and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The migration text tells consumers instructions are now usable as hash keys; nothing tells them this half of the population throws on collision.

text_a: `Parser.test` marks the deferred `secret` value without skipping it, so any JSON object with `secret` before `encoding` fails to import; this is the bug that makes the mutant unkillable.
scenario_a: `PrivateKeyEncoding.fromJsonPrivateKey(JsonIterator.parse("{\"secret\":\"<base64 private key>\",\"encoding\":\"base64PrivateKey\"}"))` throws `JsonException` instead of returning a `Signer`. `secretMark = ji.mark()` leaves the cursor at the start of the secret value and returns true, so `testObject` resumes reading a field name from inside the value and dies. All five encodings are affected (the committed test iterates all five and asserts the throw). Because the deferred path can therefore never succeed, `createSigner` is never entered with `signer == null && secretMark != 0`, which is exactly why `RemoveConditionalMutator_EQUAL_IF` on `if (secretMark == 0)` (line 137) survives and why the two `ji.reset(...)` `NakedReceiverMutator` rows stay `NO_COVERAGE`.

text_a: The new F06 javadoc states the JDK 26/27 read-ahead condition as "the inflater holds leftover input"; the actual condition is leftover input greater than 26 bytes, and the difference is exactly the case the harness relies on available() for.
scenario_a: A maintainer trims FragmentedInputStream.available() (or replaces the stream with one whose available() returns 0) on the strength of this sentence, reasoning that the inflater always holds some leftover after a member so read-ahead happens anyway. On JDK 26/27 the concatenated-member modes then silently return only the first member and fuzzHttpBody/the seed replay fails with "stream route returned the wrong body in mode 2" — the exact regression the sentence was written to prevent.
text_b: The F06 rationale states the JDK 26/27 read-ahead gate as "the source reports more bytes or the inflater holds leftover input", but the real gate is `this.in.available() > 0 || n > 26`; leftover input alone is not enough, and the 26-byte threshold is what actually forces the harness's available() to be honest.
scenario_b: A maintainer reads this javadoc and concludes that FragmentedInputStream.available() only has to be non-zero-ish, or that a pessimistic available() is safe whenever the inflater still holds bytes. text_a: The mutator has no reach into the wire bytes at all — every body handed to readBody is GZIPOutputStream output modulo three fixed one-byte edits — so the target cannot generate the one malformed shape that readBody silently accepts: a valid gzip member followed by non-member bytes.
scenario_a: A hostile or buggy provider/CDN returns `Content-Encoding: gzip` with a valid member carrying `{"result":[...` followed by any trailing bytes (padding, a truncated second member, a re-transmitted fragment). readBody returns only the first member's bytes and throws nothing, so the caller parses a silently truncated JSON-RPC document. Neither the 14 seeds nor 11,162,719 fuzz executions can reach that byte sequence, because no mode emits a valid member followed by non-member bytes, and no test in the commit pins the behaviour.
text_b: The harness's "encoding-header shape" selector models a multi-encoding response only as two separate field lines, so it cannot reach the RFC-canonical comma-joined form `Content-Encoding: identity, gzip`, which `isGzipEncoded` silently fails to recognise and hands the caller still-compressed bytes.

scenario_a: A third-party class `implements Transaction` must supply `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` because it is abstract. There is no non-deprecated method it can implement instead: `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:845) is a `default` that calls `sign(signers)`, and all five other `signInOrder*` defaults (lines 850, 855, 860, 865, 870) likewise delegate to deprecated members. text_a: The new javadoc enumerates the method's mutation of `sortedAccounts` but omits that it also mutates the caller's `LookupTableAccountMeta` objects — and does so only when two or more tables are passed.

So a caller who builds two transactions from the same `metas` array on two threads gets interleaved `reset()`/`addAccountIfExists` and two transactions whose lookup sections index the wrong accounts, while a caller who pre-populates metas and passes exactly one sees them survive — opposite behaviours from one signature, neither documented. The retired acceptance's own reasoning leans on this mutation ("the table metas already captured those lookup accounts").
text_b: Only one of the two public array-taking createTx overloads got the new in-place-mutation javadoc; the AddressLookupTable overload compacts the caller's array identically and is still undocumented — and it is the code path the documented overload's own one-table promise is delegated to.

text_a: CONVENTIONS.md claims to be the one place this family of surprises is visible, but has no entry for the createTx caller-array mutation nor for the two earlier declaration-only surprises added in this same review chain.

The file says nothing about any of them, so the contributor writes the reasonable assertion - reusing a sorted array across two createTx calls, or asserting `extraAccounts(List.of((AccountMeta) null))` appends a null - and it fails, which is precisely the failure mode the file's own preamble says it exists to prevent ("several of these were found by writing the *reasonable* assertion and watching it fail").
text_b: A newly documented caller-visible array-ownership surprise was added at the declaration but not to CONVENTIONS.md, the file whose stated purpose is to make that family visible in one place.
scenario_b: A consumer follows the file's own instruction ("Read this before writing assertions against an API you have not used here") and reads the `## Byte-array ownership` section.
